items.headline: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude proved the Riemann Hypothesis
items.summary: Levent Alpöge (@__alpoge__) posted a claimed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, written with Claude and published as a formal proof in Lean, @HarryStoltz1 flagged early Friday; @sciam called it a claim on "the most notorious open problem in all of math." @MattPirkowski noted the proof runs to more than 250,000 pages' worth of machine-checkable code, so no human, its author included, has read it end to end. @sundarpichai's "Euler, Gauss and Riemann in awe" was the most-liked reaction; by Saturday morning @elonmusk was hedging: "Even if Riemann turns out not to be fully solved yet, it will be soon enough."
items.short: A claimed AI-assisted proof of math's most famous open problem, checkable by machine but not yet read by people.

items.headline: Nvidia falls 12% on an SEC accounting report as the feed argues for Jensen's return
items.summary: Nvidia dropped about 12% Friday, a seventh straight loss, after a report that the SEC is probing its accounting, @aleabitoreddit and @MilkRoadAI posted; the stock is down more than 46% in weeks. President Trump said the board should bring Jensen Huang back, which @GavinSBaker read as a sign there are no national-security concerns. Chamath, quoted by @firesidealpha, countered that reinstating him now "throws governance out the window." @paulg: "Everyone in tech thinks the board made a huge mistake. Except the board."
items.short: SEC accounting report sinks NVDA again; Trump, Baker and Paul Graham want Jensen back, Chamath says not now.

items.headline: A week for the record books, read as a leverage unwind rather than a crisis
items.summary: The S&P 500 fell every day this week, with four declines of 1% or more, something that has happened only six times since WWII, @oguzerkan noted; @ren_stocks said the Nasdaq is on pace for its fourth-worst month since 2008 and the VIX touched 40. @oguzerkan's read: not a systemic event like 2000 or 2008, but an unwinding of leveraged long positions in the AI trade as capex expectations reset. @HyperTechInvest scored the backdrop against 2008, 2018 and 2022 and found it closest to 2018, with richer valuations.
items.short: Six-times-since-WWII losing week; the calmer take is forced selling of leveraged AI bets, closer to 2018 than 2008.

items.headline: Altimeter: Anthropic reached a ~$70B run rate on under $10B of cash burn
items.summary: Altimeter's Apoorv Agrawal, posted by @MollySOShea, said Anthropic burned less than $10 billion to reach a roughly $70 billion revenue run rate, with the compute cost of serving a dollar of revenue down from 88 cents to 15 cents. His charts put big tech's AI capex on pace for about $860 billion this year, more than tripled in two years, while AI models and apps have grown about 100x.
items.short: Compute per revenue dollar from 88¢ to 15¢; big-tech AI capex near $860B this year.

items.author: Gavin Baker
items.text:
There is real fear that Nvidia might pull back on their investments and backstops. 
 
I believe this is misplaced. Nvidia’s competitors are eager to take their place, disrupt their relationships and fill any vacuum left by Nvidia.
 
There are at least three companies aggressively vying to be the new “Central Bank” of AI.
 
Across many @atreidesmgmt venture portfolio companies we are seeing Nvidia’s semiconductor and hyperscale competitors trying to lean in and displace Nvidia in important relationships. Ironically, sometimes at more favorable terms than those offered by Nvidia.
 
And of course, also beginning to see the first signs of Nvidia waking up to this risk and addressing it. Their strategic imperatives have not changed and their strategy was sound, but there is only one Jensen and competitors are now attempting to really take advantage of his absence. No one wants a monopsony at the lab layer.
 
I suspect the same thing is happening in the supply chain. But again, there is only one Jensen.

From "regular insurance companies, et cetera"

"that the ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront"

items.author: Daniel Romero
items.text:
The question is: 

Is this 2008 🔴, 2022 🟡 or 2018 🟢?

🟢 Based on inflation, it’s closer to 2018, with a 2008-style oil shock on top

🔴 Based on long-term real yields, the cost of capital is higher than in 2018 or 2022, and near the 2008 crisis peak

🟢 Based on credit spreads, it’s far healthier than 2008 and less stressed than in 2018 or 2022

🟢 Based on GDP growth, it’s closer to 2018

🟡 Based on the labor market, it’s nothing like 2008, but looser than in 2018 or 2022

🟢 Based on S&P 500 revenue growth, it’s better than all three

🟢 Based on profit margins, it’s better than all three

🟢 Based on earnings momentum, it’s stronger than in all three, but concentrated in AI 

🔴 Based on valuations, it’s pricier than at the 2008, 2018, and 2022 lows

🔴 Based on the earnings yield minus the 10-year Treasury yield, stocks are far less attractive relative to bonds than at any of those lows

🟢 Based on bank lending standards, it’s much healthier than in 2008 or 2022, and closer to 2018

🟢 Based on the yield curve, it remains positively sloped, unlike during much of 2022

🟢 Based on ISM manufacturing and services PMIs, economic activity remains expansionary, much closer to 2018 than to the contractions seen in 2008 or late 2022

🔴 Based on the federal deficit as a share of GDP, it’s bigger than in 2018 or 2022

🟡 Based on household credit delinquencies, financial stress is elevated, particularly in credit cards, but mortgage distress remains far below 2008 levels

Conclusion: The severity of this downturn is closer to 2018, but with some elements of 2022 and the unique complexities of the AI buildout

Given the 23% Nasdaq drawdown in 2018 and the 36% drawdown in 2022, and considering we're already down 18% this time, the pain may persist for a while, but the bottom may not be far off unless macroeconomic indicators deteriorate further

items.author: Fireside Alpha
items.text:
Chamath says the over-earning era of NVIDIA may be over, and he says that is independent of Jensen

“And so you’re gonna have this really rich app ecosystem, a lot of open source models, and some closed source models, and then you’re gonna use a lot of distributed silicon.”

“This, I think, is why NVIDIA is trading down is this realization that the over-earning era of NVIDIA may be over. This is independent of Jensen, where you just have a multitude of formats and ways in which you can actually compute what you need, and then you’re gonna need this really important constraint, is the land and the power.”

“So I think if you view it that way, Jason, you’re gonna see these eight, nine, 10 conglomerates, and now the market is betting who is a conglomerate and who is not.”

“And that more than anything I think explains the flows over the last few weeks and probably like the last year even.”

quoted.author: Fireside Alpha
quoted.text:
Chamath says reinstating Jensen Huang now would throw Nvidia governance out the window and put the company at risk

“I think it’s very complicated still to have a definitive opinion beyond the following. He was an exceptional, legendary founder and CEO. He built the most important company in the most important industry in the world. He is biblically good. He also made a bunch of mistakes. The extent of those are still not known.

“And the problem is that you can’t reinstate somebody like that into a public company with that much valuation that has been destroyed, because it just completely throws governance out the window and it puts everybody at risk, everybody, including the company.

“So that’s why it’s not going to happen and that’s why they have to say that. And the unfortunate part is I think Colette is excellent, and she’s put in the awkward situation of having to be the message bearer of that. And so then you get the internet trolls that run around and give her a hard time, and it’s not her hard time. She’s just a messenger.”

items.author: Fireside Alpha
items.text:
Boring Company tunnels cost single-digit millions per mile versus $5 billion a mile for the New York City subway, according to Boring Company President Steve Davis

“So, Boring, by yards of concrete deployed, might be one of the top three infrastructure companies in America already. Vegas Loop is where we do most of our tunneling. It’s about 1.1, 1.2 million yards of concrete, 30 million yards of dirt moved, which, besides maybe Terafab and some of the chip factories, is one of the biggest infrastructure projects in the country. 70 miles of tunnel entitled.”

“Then we have Music City Loop in Nashville, which is a 20-mile project. We’re tunneling in San Antonio. We broke ground a few days ago. And then we have operations in Dubai and hope to spool one up in Orlando.”

“But the whole concept here is that the tunnels are great, and we can talk about that forever, but they typically just cost too much. New York City subway is the extreme example at $5 billion a mile. LA Metro, I believe, is around a billion a mile. They’re always over half a billion a mile, and Boring Company tunnels are single-digit millions per mile.”

“So the second you’ve brought the price down that much, all of a sudden the use cases go way up, and you start using it places you wouldn’t have used it.”

quoted.author: Fireside Alpha
quoted.text:
Boring Company President Steve Davis says Elon Musk knows the material and price of every part on every Tesla car and SpaceX rocket, and calls him "the best engineer in the world"

“It’s great. I mean, arguably the best engineer in the world. So, why would you not want to work for the best engineer in the world? I can go anecdote after anecdote after anecdote.”

“But I think the one thing that is very visible with Elon is that he knows, as you’ve seen, every minute detail of every single part on every Tesla car, on every SpaceX rocket, and he knows its purpose. And if there is no purpose, it gets deleted.”

“So, he’ll see a part and say, what’s that made of? Oh, it’s A514 steel, 100 ksi yield strength, 50 cents a pound. He’ll know all the numbers and he’ll know why it’s there.”

“And that’s something that’s really important for engineers to do. So, everyone at the Boring Company can walk up and down the boring machine. They know the material of every part, the yield strength of every part, the cost of the material, the cost of the part, the lead time for the part, the supply chain for the part, and that allows you to make good decisions.”

“That sounds super obvious, but I would challenge anyone, even at the company you’re working at. Do you know that for all of the parts? And it’s rare the answer is yes. And for Elon, the answer is unequivocally yes.”

items.title: What a 39% drawdown feels like from the inside
items.author: Daniel Koss
items.summary: An honest account of sitting through a 39% drop (after an earlier 50% one): the urge to sell and end the "psychological terror" was immense, and he names it as emotion rather than analysis. Worth reading this week less as advice to hold than as a picture of what volatility does to the body, and why the right position size is the one you can sit with.

items.headline: Reuters: SEC enforcement staff are examining Nvidia's accounting
items.summary: Two people briefed on the matter told Reuters the SEC is scrutinizing potential accounting issues at Nvidia; the SEC declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal had reported a probe earlier in the week without its focus. Nvidia closed the week down about 14%, The Verge reported. An investigation is not evidence of wrongdoing.

items.headline: Independent checkers accept the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis; human review still ahead
items.summary: Levent Alpöge's proof, written with Claude, was released as 175,187 Lean files. MIT's Andrew Sutherland reports it compiles, uses only Lean's three standard axioms and has been accepted by two independently written kernels, with the final end-to-end checks still running. There is no human-readable write-up yet, and number theorist Andrew Granville told Nature he should have prepared one before announcing.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a card is red on one side, it has a circle on the other.
items.explanation: Red could hide something that breaks the rule; Triangle breaks it if the other side turns out to be Red. Circle can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Green isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.

items.author: Andy Schoonover
items.text:
I took about 200 calls from prospective @crowdhealth customers last year. One of the biggest shocks was the number of people who said either:

"I hate my job. Want to leave. I can't because of health insurance."

or

"I can no longer do my own thing. I have to go and get a job with good health insurance because it's becoming so expensive."

My favorite conversations were:
"I'm so glad I found CrowdHealth. I'm going to join, quit my job and stay home with my babies."

My expectation is that I'll hear the same thing this year. I'm on the phone most of the day today.

items.author: Vebjørn
items.text:
I completely sold out of direct semi exposure 4 months  ago

As Buffett once said:

Rule number 1: Never lose money
Rule number 2: Never forget rule 1

That basically means avoid the large drawdowns

So I instead bought sectors that were priced for disruption, like ad-tech, SaaS and mobility (with hyperscalers as core positions still)

As a result my portfolio has kept its 2x S&P 500 CAGR despite a tech heavy drop (Nasdaq down 20% so far)

My portfolio has a 24.8% CAGR vs 12% for $SPY over the same period

Risk management is boring until it saves your ass

items.author: The Kobeissi Letter
items.text:
BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, sets a new record for the largest-ever loss of market cap in a stock in 45 days.

The stock has now lost -$2.8 trillion in market cap from its high seen on October 6th.

There have been 33 trading days since October 6th, meaning Nvidia has lost an average of -$85 billion per day, for 33 trading days in a row.

Furthermore, Nvidia has accounted for ~40% of the S&P 500's market cap losses since its record high on October 6th.

That's one way to make history.

items.author: Ren
items.text:
VIX hit 40 today, even if just for a few seconds.

Historically, this is when you want to go back into growth names aggressively.

But we don't know where the bottom is yet, so the most sensible thing is to add slowly to the names you love. That's what I'm doing, DCA one step at a time.

Quality names compound regardless of macro.

And with $NVDA at $130, I might even tap into options, the lower it goes the more attractive it will be.
